read.sections.0.heading.source: From rules to learning from text
read.sections.0.heading.back: From rules to learning from text

read.sections.0.text.source: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules that people wrote. Today, many chatbots are built on a large language model, or LLM, which uses machine learning instead. An LLM learns patterns from a huge amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages, much of it written by people. LLMs grew from the same things as the photo programs in Lesson 2: lots of digital data and fast chips. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks, and many later LLMs were built on it. In November 2022, the company OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot built on an LLM.
read.sections.0.text.back: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules written by people. Today, many chatbots are built on a large language model, or LLM, which uses machine learning instead. An LLM learns patterns from a very large amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages, and most of it was written by people. LLMs grew from the same things as the photo programs in Lesson 2: lots of digital data and fast chips. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks, and many later LLMs were built on it. In November 2022, the company OpenAI launched ChatGPT, a chatbot built on an LLM.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How it writes, one piece at a time
read.sections.1.heading.back: How it writes, one piece at a time

read.sections.1.text.source: An LLM works with small pieces of text called tokens. A token may be a word or part of a word. Suppose a learner asks, “What is a map scale?” The model predicts a likely first token, such as “A”. It adds it, then predicts the next one, such as “map”, using everything written so far. It goes on, piece by piece, until the answer is finished. A toy example shows the idea. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came after “a cup of” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once. Real models do not just count words; they learn far richer patterns from far more text. Often each token is picked partly by chance from the likely ones, so the same question can get different answers. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time.
read.sections.1.text.back: An LLM works with small pieces of text, called tokens. A token may be a word or part of a word. Suppose a learner asks, “What is a map scale?” The model predicts a likely first token, such as “Scale”. It adds it, then predicts the next token, such as “map”, using everything already written. It goes on like this, piece by piece, until the answer is finished. A simple example shows this idea. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came after “a cup of” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once. Real models do not just count words; they learn far richer patterns from far more text. Often each token is picked partly at random from the likely tokens, so the same question can get different answers. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time.
read.sections.1.text.note: The English answer starts “A”, then “map” (“A map scale is …”). A Malay answer starts “Skala peta …” (scale map), so the example tokens are “Skala”, then “peta”; the glossary examples use “peta” too.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Why it matters for writing, translation and information
read.sections.2.heading.back: Why this matters for writing, translation and information

read.sections.2.text.source: LLMs are now used to help people write, translate and look for information. A chatbot can explain an idea in simpler words, help with a first draft or translate a short notice. At Lakeside, a teacher checked the helper's explanation, and it was right. A volunteer fixed two words in its translation. Many LLMs learned mainly from English, and researchers have found they usually work worse in languages with little writing online. A basic LLM predicts words that sound right; nothing in that checks the facts. So it can make things up and still sound confident, like the Lakeside helper that named a book that does not exist. Some tools also search the web and show links, but the pages can be wrong or misread. Check important answers with a trusted source, such as a library or a teacher.

watch.summary.source: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a huge amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, worked out very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts which letter often comes after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer pieces, like whole words, its guesses get much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped to make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.
watch.summary.back: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One of them works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a very large amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, calculated very fast. The video shows one small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts the letters that often come after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer bits, like whole words, its guesses become much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.

educatorNotes.0.source: There is no real chatbot in the app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are made up. The cup-of-tea game is a toy analogy, not how real models work: real LLMs learn far richer patterns over tokens from far more text, and keep no table of counts. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so the lesson says “much of it”. A model can repeat an answer: an app can pick the likeliest token every time, or pick at random among likely ones (Google's course).
